# Where this goes

## Splitting it up

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
- Censoring was the first piece. It is now one package among several,
  all of them wrappers over `Distributions.jl`
- `ConvolvedDistributions.jl` does the sum of independent delays, with
  closed forms where they exist and the same fixed node quadrature
  where they do not, plus differences, products and ratios
- `DistributionsInference.jl` turns a distribution into a
  `LogDensityProblems` problem once you write `parameter_rows` and
  `reconstruct` for it. Today only `ComposedDistributions.jl` has those
  shipped
- The example on the right is plain `Distributions.jl` dispatch. Where
  the two packages do talk to each other it is through one package
  extension, not a hard dependency
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
```julia
using CensoredDistributions
using ConvolvedDistributions, Distributions

incubation = Gamma(2.0, 1.0)
reporting = LogNormal(1.0, 0.5)

d = convolved(incubation, reporting)
observed = double_interval_censored(
    d; upper = 15, interval = 1
)

cdf(observed, 5.0)   # 0.4561
```

::: {.attribution}
Composed for this talk rather than lifted from a README, which is the
point of the slide. Run against `CensoredDistributions.jl` v0.2.22 and
`ConvolvedDistributions.jl`
:::
:::
::::

## epidist, composed

- `epidist` is our R package for fitting delay distributions. It sits
  on `primarycensored` and on `brms`, and it is where partial pooling
  and flexible delay shapes live
- The Julia version is a composed one. `CensoredDistributions.jl` for
  the observation process, Turing submodels for the rest
- Partial pooling across strata, so a delay estimated by age group or
  by region borrows strength instead of being fitted on its own
- Flexible delay shapes, so the delay is not forced to be a gamma or a
  lognormal
- None of it is written yet. The generation time is the same shape of
  problem, a convolution and a difference and a censoring adjustment
  stacked, and `GenerationTime.jl` is an empty repository

::: {.attribution}
Open issue `CensoredDistributions.jl#749` says the joint fit is too
slow, because reverse mode autodiff through `cdf(Convolved(...))` costs
too much per leapfrog step.
:::

## What I would use today

- If you estimate delays in R, use `primarycensored`. It works, it is on
  CRAN, and there are packages built on top of it
- If you are writing a model in Julia, the composition is worth more
  than the package. Any distribution, any sampler, no integer tables
- Multiple dispatch removed a class of bug that R and Stan could only
  write a test for
- It did not remove the numerical problem. That moved to a list of
  which autodiff backends work

::: {.callout-important}
The composition is the reusable part. The package is only where the
censoring happens to live.
:::
